name: GSK-2849466
lead: GSK-2849466 (GSK2849466) is an investigational non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the N-arylhydroxyalkyl class, developed by GlaxoSmithKline and investigated for cachexia and heart failure.[1] SARMs are designed to switch on the androgen receptor in muscle and bone while sparing tissues such as the prostate, which is why they attract people who want more muscle mass without the profile of testosterone.[1]

For a lifter, the interest in a SARM is the possibility of added lean mass and strength from an oral compound; the broader class has shown increases in lean body mass in trials, as with enobosarm, which raised lean body mass in a phase III trial without significantly improving physical function.[1] GSK2849466 itself reached only a small Phase I trial and was discontinued, so no efficacy or body-composition data exist for it.[1][2]

The registered Phase I trial, NCT01696604, started on 26 September 2012, enrolled 17 healthy men to evaluate safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, and is listed as completed with cachexia as the associated condition.[2] It is not an approved drug and is not a mainstream product in the SARM market.

chain: Selective activation of the androgen receptor in muscle and bone
Claimed gain in muscle size and strength
angle.text: As a SARM, it was designed to build or preserve muscle in conditions like cachexia. The idea that a drug of this type adds muscle is the basis of its interest to lifters, but no results for this specific compound have been published.

infobox: Not approved; investigational. SARMs are prohibited by WADA since 2008[1]

paras: Wikipedia lists GSK2849466 as a GlaxoSmithKline compound that reached Phase I and was discontinued.[1] Its registered trial started on 26 September 2012 and enrolled 17 healthy men.[2]

SARMs have been studied for osteoporosis, cachexia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, stress urinary incontinence, breast cancer, muscular dystrophy, hypogonadism and male contraception; as of 2023 none had been approved by the FDA or EMA.[1] Proposed advantages over testosterone include oral bioavailability and no conversion to oestrogen.[1]

Enobosarm is the most-studied SARM, and in a phase III trial it increased lean body mass without significantly improving physical function.[1] Trial adverse events for the class were generally mild and infrequent, with raised liver enzymes, lower HDL cholesterol and dose-dependent falls in testosterone reported, and case reports link recreational use to liver injury.[1] The World Anti-Doping Agency has prohibited SARMs since 2008.[1]

One Phase I trial (NCT01696604, n=17, healthy males, 2012) assessed safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics and is listed as completed.[2] No results have been published and no efficacy trial has been reported.

timeline.event: Phase I trial of GSK2849466 in healthy men begins (26 September).[2]

quick.overview:
GSK-2849466 is an experimental SARM from GlaxoSmithKline, studied for cachexia and heart failure.

It was tested in one small Phase I trial of 17 healthy men and then discontinued.
quick.mechanism: It is meant to activate androgen receptors preferentially in muscle and bone rather than reproductive tissue, and belongs to the N-arylhydroxyalkyl class.
quick.risks: No trial results are published in the sources reviewed. The SARM class is unapproved, banned by WADA, and associated in case reports with liver injury from recreational use.
